beats.text: The cells of innate immunity. The exam asks where each cell comes from, how NK cells pick a target, and how mast cells differ from eosinophils.
beats.no_facts_reason: Intro and overview; facts follow in later beats.
beats.visual: Title card; three exam hooks appear.
beats.say: The cells of innate immunity. The exam asks where each cell comes from, how N K cells pick a target, and how mast cells differ from eosinophils.

beats.text: Every blood cell starts from one haematopoietic stem cell, or HSC, in the bone marrow. HSCs carry CD34 and c-KIT.
beats.visual: Lineage tree root: HSC in bone marrow, CD34, c-KIT.
beats.say: Every blood cell starts from one haematopoietic stem cell, or H S C, in the bone marrow. H S Cs carry C D 34 and C kit.

beats.text: The myeloid branch makes neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils and monocytes. Most dendritic cells come from a precursor shared with monocytes.
beats.visual: Myeloid branch grows: neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, monocyte, DC.

beats.text: Mast cells leave the marrow as progenitors and mature in the tissues. Basophils mature in the marrow, from different progenitors.
beats.visual: Mast cell progenitor exits the marrow into tissue; basophil stays inside.

beats.text: The lymphoid branch makes T cells, B cells, and a shared precursor of natural killer cells and innate lymphoid cells, or ILCs.
beats.visual: Lymphoid branch grows: T, B, NK and ILC.
beats.say: The lymphoid branch makes T cells, B cells, and a shared precursor of natural killer cells and innate lymphoid cells, or I L Cs.

beats.text: Each line has a growth factor: G-CSF for neutrophils, M-CSF for monocytes, FLT3 ligand for dendritic cells, IL-5 for eosinophils, and SCF for mast cells.
beats.visual: Growth-factor tags pin onto the tree leaves.
beats.say: Each line has a growth factor: G C S F for neutrophils, M C S F for monocytes, F L T 3 ligand for dendritic cells, I L 5 for eosinophils, and S C F for mast cells.

beats.text: The neutrophil is the most abundant white blood cell, 40 to 60 percent of leukocytes. Its nucleus has three to five lobes, so we call it a polymorphonuclear leukocyte.
beats.visual: Neutrophil with multi-lobed nucleus; PMN label.

beats.text: Most granules are specific granules, with lysozyme, collagenase and elastase. Azurophilic granules hold myeloperoxidase, defensins and cathelicidins.
beats.visual: Two granule types with content lists.

beats.text: Neutrophils act fast, with preformed enzymes, but live only one to two days in tissues. Macrophages respond more slowly, and often need new gene transcription.
beats.visual: Speed comparison: neutrophil vs macrophage.

beats.text: Neutrophils can throw out their nuclear contents as nets, neutrophil extracellular traps. Nets trap and kill microbes, but can also damage healthy tissue.
beats.visual: Web of NET strands catches microbes.

beats.text: Classical monocytes are 90 to 95 percent of blood monocytes. They rush to infection and become macrophages. But most tissue-resident macrophages come from yolk sac or fetal liver precursors, and renew themselves.
beats.visual: Monocyte becomes macrophage; fetal origin of resident macrophages.

beats.text: Examples are Kupffer cells in the liver, alveolar macrophages in the lung and microglia in the brain.
beats.visual: Three resident macrophages: liver, lung, brain.

beats.text: Two source conflicts. Janeway says tissue macrophages mature from blood monocytes, and dendritic cells also have a lymphoid origin. Abbas is newer, so use Abbas for the exam.
beats.visual: Abbas vs Janeway note.

beats.text: Macrophages make cytokines such as TNF and IL-1. They clear apoptotic cells, called efferocytosis. Their receptor SIRP alpha reads CD47, a don't eat me signal on healthy cells.
beats.visual: Macrophage with three jobs; CD47 sign.
beats.say: Macrophages make cytokines such as T N F and I L 1. They clear apoptotic cells, called efferocytosis. Their receptor sirp alpha reads C D 47, a don't eat me signal on healthy cells.

beats.text: Lipopolysaccharide and interferon gamma give classical M1 macrophages that kill microbes. IL-4 and IL-13 drive alternative M2 macrophages for repair and fibrosis. Many macrophages fit neither box.
beats.visual: Fork: M1 kill vs M2 repair.
beats.say: Lipopolysaccharide and interferon gamma give classical M1 macrophages that kill microbes. I L 4 and I L 13 drive alternative M2 macrophages for repair and fibrosis. Many macrophages fit neither box.

beats.text: Dendritic cells are sentinels. They capture antigens in tissues and carry them to lymph nodes. There, they direct naive T cells to become effector cells, such as Th1 or Th17 cells.
beats.visual: DC carries antigen to lymph node; T cell to Th1/Th17.
beats.say: Dendritic cells are sentinels. They capture antigens in tissues and carry them to lymph nodes. There, they direct naive T cells to become effector cells, such as T H 1 or T H 17 cells.

beats.text: cDC2 cells are the most numerous, and present antigen mainly to CD4 T cells. cDC1 cells cross-present antigen to naive CD8 T cells, and make IL-12.
beats.visual: Subset cards: cDC2 to CD4, cDC1 to CD8.
beats.say: C D C 2 cells are the most numerous, and present antigen mainly to C D 4 T cells. C D C 1 cells cross-present antigen to naive C D 8 T cells, and make I L 12.

beats.text: Plasmacytoid DCs carry high TLR7 and TLR9. They are the main source of antiviral type I interferon. Langerhans cells are the dendritic cells of the epidermis.
beats.visual: pDC card; Langerhans card.
beats.say: Plasmacytoid D Cs carry high T L R 7 and T L R 9. They are the main source of antiviral type one interferon. Langerhans cells are the dendritic cells of the epidermis.

beats.text: Exam trap: follicular dendritic cells are stromal cells. They do not come from bone marrow, and do not present protein antigens to T cells.
beats.visual: FDC card crossed out as 'not a DC'.

beats.text: Natural killer cells are CD56 positive and CD3 negative. They kill without prior activation, using germline-encoded receptors. So they kill virus-infected cells before cytotoxic T cells are fully active.
beats.visual: NK cell with tags; timeline NK early vs CTL later.
beats.say: Natural killer cells are C D 56 positive and C D 3 negative. They kill without prior activation, using germline-encoded receptors. So they kill virus-infected cells before cytotoxic T cells are fully active.

beats.text: Perforin helps granzymes enter the target, and granzymes trigger apoptosis. NK cells also secrete interferon gamma, which activates macrophages.
beats.visual: Kill arm and IFN-gamma arm.
beats.say: Perforin helps granzymes enter the target, and granzymes trigger apoptosis. N K cells also secrete interferon gamma, which activates macrophages.

beats.text: Each NK cell weighs activating against inhibitory signals. Think of it like a balance scale. Inhibitory receptors use ITIMs, and activating receptors use ITAMs.
beats.visual: Balance scale: inhibitory vs activating pans.
beats.say: Each N K cell weighs activating against inhibitory signals. Think of it like a balance scale. Inhibitory receptors use I T I Ms, and activating receptors use I T A Ms.

beats.text: Inhibitory KIRs and CD94 NKG2A recognise MHC class I. The activating receptor NKG2D binds stress proteins on infected and tumour cells.
beats.visual: Receptors load each pan.
beats.say: Inhibitory K I Rs and C D 94 N K G 2 A recognise M H C class one. The activating receptor N K G 2 D binds stress proteins on infected and tumour cells.

beats.text: A healthy cell shows MHC class I, so inhibition wins and the NK cell walks away.
beats.visual: Healthy target: scale tips to inhibition.
beats.say: A healthy cell shows M H C class one, so inhibition wins and the N K cell walks away.

beats.text: Viruses, cell stress and many cancers reduce MHC class I. The brake is gone, the scale tips, and the NK cell kills. This is recognition of missing self.
beats.visual: MHC-I disappears; scale tips; 'missing self'.
beats.say: Viruses, cell stress and many cancers reduce M H C class one. The brake is gone, the scale tips, and the N K cell kills. This is recognition of missing self.

beats.text: CD16 binds IgG1 and IgG3 on a coated cell, and the NK cell kills it. This is antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, or ADCC.
beats.visual: IgG-coated target bound by CD16.
beats.say: C D 16 binds I g G 1 and I g G 3 on a coated cell, and the N K cell kills it. This is antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, or A D C C.

beats.text: NK cell deficiency gives severe herpesvirus and papillomavirus infections. Causes include GATA2 mutations, CD16 mutations, and Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
beats.visual: Pink clinical box: NK deficiency.
beats.say: N K cell deficiency gives severe herpesvirus and papillomavirus infections. Causes include gata 2 mutations, C D 16 mutations, and Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

beats.text: Now the allergy trio: mast cells, basophils and eosinophils. All three have granules full of mediators, and all three take part in allergic disease.
beats.visual: Three cells side by side.

beats.text: Mast cells are not in the blood. They sit near vessels and nerves, and beneath epithelia. Stem cell factor binds c-KIT and is essential for their development.
beats.visual: Mast cell by vessel and nerve; SCF to c-KIT.
beats.say: Mast cells are not in the blood. They sit near vessels and nerves, and beneath epithelia. Stem cell factor binds C kit and is essential for their development.

beats.text: The high-affinity IgE receptor, F C epsilon R one, holds IgE so tightly that most mast cells carry IgE, even in nonatopic people. It is high on mast cells and basophils, but low on eosinophils.
beats.visual: FcεRI with IgE; high/high/low bars.
beats.say: The high-affinity I g E receptor, F C epsilon R one, holds I g E so tightly that most mast cells carry I g E, even in nonatopic people. It is high on mast cells and basophils, but low on eosinophils.

beats.text: Allergen cross-links the IgE. The mast cell releases histamine and tryptase, then makes prostaglandin D2, leukotrienes and platelet-activating factor.
beats.visual: Cross-link; preformed vs new mediators.
beats.say: Allergen cross-links the I g E. The mast cell releases histamine and tryptase, then makes prostaglandin D 2, leukotrienes and platelet-activating factor.

beats.text: Mast cells also fire without IgE. C3a and C5a cause degranulation. On skin mast cells, MRGPRX2 binds some drugs and likely causes some allergy-like drug reactions.
beats.visual: Non-IgE triggers.
beats.say: Mast cells also fire without I g E. C 3 a and C 5 a cause degranulation. On skin mast cells, M R G P R X 2 binds some drugs and likely causes some allergy-like drug reactions.

beats.text: Tryptase is in all human mast cells and no other known cell. So serum tryptase helps diagnose anaphylaxis. Systemic mastocytosis is linked to c-KIT mutations.
beats.visual: Tryptase box; mastocytosis.
beats.say: Tryptase is in all human mast cells and no other known cell. So serum tryptase helps diagnose anaphylaxis. Systemic mastocytosis is linked to C kit mutations.

beats.text: Basophils are blood granulocytes, normally absent from tissues. Like mast cells, they bind IgE and fire when antigen binds it.
beats.visual: Basophil in vessel.
beats.say: Basophils are blood granulocytes, normally absent from tissues. Like mast cells, they bind I g E and fire when antigen binds it.

beats.text: Eosinophils need IL-5 from Th2 cells and ILC2s. Eotaxin binds CCR3 and recruits them. Major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein damage helminths and host cells.
beats.visual: Eosinophil with IL-5, CCR3 and granules.
beats.say: Eosinophils need I L 5 from T H 2 cells and I L C 2s. Eotaxin binds C C R 3 and recruits them. Major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein damage helminths and host cells.

beats.text: Exam trap: the eosinophil IgE receptor is low and lacks the signalling chain. There is no convincing evidence that IgE activates eosinophils.
beats.visual: Comparison bars; trap stamp.
beats.say: Exam trap: the eosinophil I g E receptor is low and lacks the signalling chain. There is no convincing evidence that I g E activates eosinophils.

beats.text: Innate lymphoid cells have no T-cell receptors. They secrete cytokines like helper T cells, and live mainly in mucosa such as lung and intestine.
beats.visual: ILC with 'no TCR'.

beats.text: ILC1s use T-bet and make interferon gamma. ILC2s use GATA3 and make IL-5 and IL-13. ILC3s use ROR gamma t and make IL-22 or IL-17.
beats.visual: Three-row ILC table.
beats.say: I L C 1s use T bet and make interferon gamma. I L C 2s use gata 3 and make I L 5 and I L 13. I L C 3s use R O R gamma t and make I L 22 or I L 17.

beats.text: In allergy, epithelial IL-25, IL-33 and TSLP activate ILC2s. ILC2s already sit in the tissue, so they can start allergic inflammation before Th2 cells arrive.
beats.visual: Epithelium releases alarmins; ILC2 first, Th2 later.
beats.say: In allergy, epithelial I L 25, I L 33 and T S L P activate I L C 2s. I L C 2s already sit in the tissue, so they can start allergic inflammation before T H 2 cells arrive.

beats.text: Five things to remember. One: all innate cells come from the HSC. Two: most tissue macrophages come from fetal precursors. Three: plasmacytoid DCs make type I interferon.
beats.visual: Recap items 1-3.
beats.say: Five things to remember. One: all innate cells come from the H S C. Two: most tissue macrophages come from fetal precursors. Three: plasmacytoid D Cs make type one interferon.

beats.text: Four: NK cells kill when MHC class I is missing. Five: ILC2s start allergic inflammation early.
beats.visual: Recap items 4-5.
beats.say: Four: N K cells kill when M H C class one is missing. Five: I L C 2s start allergic inflammation early.

beats.text: One exam trap. CD16 on NK cells binds IgG, not IgE. Next: how cells sense danger.
beats.visual: Trap card; 'Next' card.
beats.say: One exam trap. C D 16 on N K cells binds I g G, not I g E. Next: how cells sense danger.
